Vignette: Adaeze

Adaeze is a 68-year-old Nigerian-born woman who has been married to her current husband for eleven years. She sits in the chair across from her therapist with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her posture careful and contained, as though she has spent decades practicing the art of taking up as little space as possible. In many ways, she has.

For most of her adult life, Adaeze was married to a man she describes simply as "the first one." She does not say his name. The marriage lasted twenty-two years, and for nearly all of those years, he beat her — with his hands, with a belt, once with the wooden handle of a cooking spoon that left a scar along her left forearm she still covers with long sleeves, even in summer. She grew up in a community where a woman's suffering inside her home was considered private, even sacred, and so she kept it private. She raised three children, cooked, cleaned, attended church every Sunday, and told no one. When people asked about a bruise, she had an answer ready before they finished the question.

He died of a heart attack in 2007. She remembers standing at his graveside and feeling nothing, and then feeling ashamed of feeling nothing, and then spending years trying to sort out which of those feelings was the more honest one.

She eventually remarried — a gentle, patient man named Emeka — and moved with him to the United Kingdom, where they have lived quietly ever since. She has not worked since leaving Nigeria, and the stillness of her days, which she once imagined would feel like rest, has instead given the past more room to move around in.

The trouble, as Adaeze describes it, began in earnest about three years ago, though she suspects it was always there, simply waiting. She started waking at two or three in the morning with her heart pounding and her nightgown soaked through, certain she had heard something — a door, a footstep, a shift in the air pressure of the room. She lies rigid until dawn, listening. During the day, she finds herself watching Emeka's hands when he gestures while talking, tracking the arc of his movements before she can stop herself. She knows, intellectually, that he has never once raised a hand to her. This knowledge does not reach the part of her that watches his hands.

She avoids the kitchen when she is alone. She cannot fully explain this, only that the kitchen was where most of it happened, and that even the smell of certain foods — groundnut soup, fried plantain — can pull her back so completely that she has to grip the counter to remember what year it is and where she is standing.

She does not speak of any of this to Emeka. She worries that naming it would make her seem broken, or ungrateful, or like a woman who cannot leave the past in the past. Her children, now grown and scattered across two continents, call regularly and ask how she is, and she tells them she is fine. She has been telling people she is fine for so long that she sometimes wonders if she knows what the alternative would even look like.

What brought her to therapy was not a crisis but a quiet conversation with her GP, who noticed during a routine visit that her blood pressure had been climbing and asked, gently, whether there was anything worrying her. Something about the directness of the question, or perhaps simply the fact that someone had asked, caused her to cry in a way she had not cried in years — without warning, without control, without a story ready.

She is here now, hands folded, watching the door. She says she is not sure she has anything useful to say. Then she begins to talk.
